questions.q: The diagram represents two samples of gas, one of O₂ and one of CO₂. Which statement about the two samples shown is correct?
options: Both of the samples of gas have equal total masses.
The two samples contain equal amounts in moles.
The CO₂ sample contains the greater amount in moles.
The two samples contain the same number of atoms.
optionWhy: A student who thinks equal numbers of particles have equal masses picks this. A CO₂ molecule (44.01 amu) has a greater mass than an O₂ molecule (32.00 amu), so six CO₂ molecules have the greater mass.

Each box contains six molecules. The amount of a substance in moles counts particles (1 mol is 6.022 × 10²³ particles), so equal numbers of molecules are equal amounts in moles, even though the CO₂ molecules are heavier.
A student who treats the amount in moles as a measure of mass picks this. The CO₂ sample has the greater mass, but both boxes contain six molecules, so the amounts in moles are equal.
A student who equates the number of atoms with the number of molecules picks this. Each O₂ molecule has two atoms and each CO₂ molecule has three, so the boxes contain 12 and 18 atoms.
questions.explain: Each box contains six molecules. The amount of a substance in moles counts particles (1 mol is 6.022 × 10²³ particles), so equal numbers of molecules are equal amounts in moles, even though the CO₂ molecules are heavier.

questions.q: A student needs to find the mass of 0.250 mol of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, whose molar mass is 180.16 g/mol. Which relationship should she use, where m is the mass of the sample, n is the amount in moles, M is the molar mass and N_A is Avogadro's number?
options: m = n/M
m = nN_A
m = M
m = nM
optionWhy: A student who swaps the multiplication and division in n = m/M picks this. The units give mol ÷ (g/mol) = mol²/g, not grams; the mass is nM.
A student who thinks Avogadro's number converts moles to grams picks this. nN_A is the number of molecules in the sample, 1.51 × 10²³; the molar mass converts moles to grams.
A student who confuses the molar mass with the mass of the sample picks this. 180.16 g is the mass of 1 mol of glucose; 0.250 mol has a quarter of that mass.
From n = m/M, the mass is m = nM: 0.250 mol × 180.16 g/mol = 45.0 g. The units cancel to grams, which confirms the relationship.
questions.explain: From n = m/M, the mass is m = nM: 0.250 mol × 180.16 g/mol = 45.0 g. The units cancel to grams, which confirms the relationship.
questions.working: n = m/M, so m = nM = (0.250 mol)(180.16 g/mol) = 45.0 g. N_A is not needed: it converts moles to a number of molecules, not to a mass.

questions.q: A student plans to make iron(II) sulfide, FeS, by heating iron with sulfur. She wants to start with equal numbers of Fe atoms and S atoms, but atoms cannot be counted directly in the laboratory. Which procedure is best aligned with her aim?
options: Weigh out equal masses of Fe and S, such as 10.0 g of each
Measure out equal volumes of powdered Fe and powdered S
Weigh out masses of Fe and S in the ratio 55.85 g : 32.06 g
Weigh out masses of Fe and S in the ratio 26 g : 16 g
optionWhy: A student who thinks equal masses contain equal numbers of atoms picks this. An Fe atom has a greater mass than an S atom, so 10.0 g of Fe contains fewer atoms (0.179 mol) than 10.0 g of S (0.312 mol).

A student who thinks equal volumes of any two substances contain equal numbers of particles picks this. The atoms of the two solids differ in mass and pack differently, so equal volumes do not give equal numbers of atoms.

One mole of Fe atoms has a mass of 55.85 g and one mole of S atoms has a mass of 32.06 g, and a mole of any element contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. Masses in the ratio 55.85 : 32.06 therefore contain equal numbers of atoms, which is how a balance is used to count atoms.

A student who uses atomic numbers as the relative masses of atoms picks this. 26 and 16 are the numbers of protons in Fe and S atoms; the relative masses of the atoms are the atomic masses, 55.85 and 32.06, so 26 g of Fe (0.466 mol) contains about 7% fewer atoms than 16 g of S (0.499 mol).
questions.explain: One mole of Fe atoms has a mass of 55.85 g and one mole of S atoms has a mass of 32.06 g, and a mole of any element contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. Masses in the ratio 55.85 : 32.06 therefore contain equal numbers of atoms, which is how a balance is used to count atoms.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of a sample of neon, Ne, shows three peaks, at masses of 20 amu, 21 amu and 22 amu. Which statement about the atoms in the sample is correct?
options: Atoms with 20, 21 and 22 protons per nucleus are present.
Ne atoms with 10, 11 and 12 electrons are present.
Atoms with 10, 11 and 12 protons in their nuclei are present.
Ne atoms with 10, 11 and 12 neutrons are present.
optionWhy: A student who reads the mass of an isotope as its number of protons picks this. The mass in amu is close to the mass number, protons plus neutrons; an atom with 20 protons would be calcium, not neon.
A student who thinks isotopes differ in their numbers of electrons picks this. Neutral atoms of every Ne isotope have 10 electrons; the isotopes differ in neutrons, which changes the mass.

A student who thinks isotopes differ in their numbers of protons picks this. Atoms with 11 or 12 protons would be sodium or magnesium; all isotopes of neon have 10 protons and differ in their numbers of neutrons.
Every Ne atom has 10 protons (atomic number 10). The three peaks are isotopes with mass numbers 20, 21 and 22, so the atoms have 20 − 10 = 10, 11 and 12 neutrons.
questions.explain: Every Ne atom has 10 protons (atomic number 10). The three peaks are isotopes with mass numbers 20, 21 and 22, so the atoms have 20 − 10 = 10, 11 and 12 neutrons.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of a sample of a hypothetical element X is shown. Based on the spectrum, which statement about the average atomic mass of X in the sample is correct?
options: It is between 50 amu and 51 amu.
It is between 51 and 52 amu.
It is exactly 51 amu, the midpoint.
It is 50 amu, the top peak's mass.
optionWhy: 70% of the atoms have a mass of 50 amu and 30% have a mass of 52 amu, so the weighted average is 0.70 × 50 + 0.30 × 52 = 50.6 amu. The average lies closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope, between 50 amu and 51 amu.

A student who thinks the heavier isotope counts for more in a weighted average picks this. Each isotope counts in proportion to its abundance; the lighter isotope is the more abundant (70%), so the average, 50.6 amu, lies closer to 50 amu.

A student who takes the simple mean of the two isotope masses picks this. 51 amu would be the average only if the isotopes were equally abundant; here 70% of the atoms are the lighter isotope, so the average is 50.6 amu.
A student who takes the mass of the most abundant isotope as the average atomic mass picks this. The 30% of atoms with a mass of 52 amu raise the average above 50 amu, to 50.6 amu.
questions.explain: 70% of the atoms have a mass of 50 amu and 30% have a mass of 52 amu, so the weighted average is 0.70 × 50 + 0.30 × 52 = 50.6 amu. The average lies closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope, between 50 amu and 51 amu.
questions.working: Weighted average = 0.70 × 50 amu + 0.30 × 52 amu = 35.0 + 15.6 = 50.6 amu, which lies between 50 amu and 51 amu.

questions.q: Boron has two stable isotopes, ¹⁰B (10.01 amu) and ¹¹B (11.01 amu). A sample of boron is prepared in which 90.0% of the atoms are ¹¹B. Which value is closest to the average atomic mass of boron in this sample, in amu?
optionWhy: A student who takes the simple mean of the two isotope masses picks this. The isotopes are not equally abundant: 90.0% of the atoms are ¹¹B, so the average is much closer to 11.01 amu.

A student who thinks the average atomic mass is fixed for an element picks this, the periodic-table value for natural boron. That value applies to natural boron (about 80% ¹¹B); this sample, with 90.0% ¹¹B, has a greater average atomic mass.

The weighted average for this sample is 0.900 × 11.01 + 0.100 × 10.01 = 10.91 amu. It is greater than the periodic-table value for boron, 10.81, because this sample contains a larger fraction of the heavier isotope than natural boron.
A student who takes the mass of the most abundant isotope as the average atomic mass picks this. The 10.0% of atoms that are ¹⁰B lower the average to 10.9 amu.
questions.explain: The weighted average for this sample is 0.900 × 11.01 + 0.100 × 10.01 = 10.91 amu. It is greater than the periodic-table value for boron, 10.81, because this sample contains a larger fraction of the heavier isotope than natural boron.

questions.q: Which of the numbered diagrams best represents the arrangement of particles in a small part of a sample of solid sodium chloride, NaCl? Charges are not shown.
options: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks ionic compounds consist of molecules picks this. The diagram shows separate Na–Cl pairs; solid NaCl has no separate pairs, but an extended array in which each ion is surrounded by ions of the other element.
A student who thinks a compound contains molecules of its elements picks this. The chlorine in NaCl is present as separate chloride ions, not as Cl–Cl pairs.

NaCl is an ionic compound: Na and Cl particles (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions) are held in a 1 : 1 ratio in an extended array, each surrounded by particles of the other kind, with no separate molecules. The diagram in which Na and Cl alternate in every row and column shows this.

A student who thinks a compound is a mixture of its elements picks this. The diagram shows sodium and chlorine still uncombined, a mixture of the two elements; in NaCl the elements are combined in a fixed ratio.
questions.explain: NaCl is an ionic compound: Na and Cl particles (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions) are held in a 1 : 1 ratio in an extended array, each surrounded by particles of the other kind, with no separate molecules. The diagram in which Na and Cl alternate in every row and column shows this.

questions.q: A student has found the empirical formula of a molecular compound from its percent composition by mass. Which additional quantity does the student need in order to determine the compound's molecular formula?
options: None; the empirical formula is also the molecular formula
The total mass of the sample of the compound analyzed
The molar mass of the compound, found by another method
The atomic numbers of the elements in the compound
optionWhy: A student who thinks the empirical formula is the formula of an actual molecule picks this. Different compounds share an empirical formula (CH₂O and C₂H₄O₂), so the empirical formula alone does not give the molecular formula.

A student who thinks percent composition depends on the size of the sample picks this. Every sample of the compound has the same percent composition, so the sample mass gives no information about the size of the molecule.

The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Dividing the compound's molar mass by the mass of the empirical formula gives that multiple; percent composition alone cannot, because CH₂O and C₂H₄O₂ have the same composition.

A student who thinks atomic numbers give the masses of atoms picks this. Atomic numbers count protons; the atomic masses were already used to find the empirical formula, and the missing quantity is the molar mass.
questions.explain: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Dividing the compound's molar mass by the mass of the empirical formula gives that multiple; percent composition alone cannot, because CH₂O and C₂H₄O₂ have the same composition.
questions.working: The molecular formula is n × (empirical formula), where n = (molar mass of compound)/(mass of one empirical formula unit). Only the molar mass is needed in addition to the empirical formula.

questions.q: The table gives the results of analyses of two samples of pure carbon dioxide, CO₂. What is the mass of carbon in sample 2?
optionWhy: A student who thinks every sample of a compound contains the same mass of each element picks this. Every sample has the same proportion of carbon; sample 2 is 2.50 times as massive, so it contains 2.50 times as much carbon.
Every sample of CO₂ has the same mass ratio of C to CO₂: 1.20/4.40 = 0.273. Sample 2 is 2.50 times as massive as sample 1, so it contains 2.50 × 1.20 g = 3.00 g of carbon.
A student who takes the mass fraction of carbon to be its atom fraction, 1 of the 3 atoms in CO₂, picks this. A C atom has less mass than an O atom, so carbon is only 27.3% of the mass of CO₂.

A student who adds the extra 6.6 g of sample 2 to the mass of carbon picks this. The masses of the elements scale in proportion to the sample mass, by a factor of 2.50, not by adding the same number of grams.
questions.explain: Every sample of CO₂ has the same mass ratio of C to CO₂: 1.20/4.40 = 0.273. Sample 2 is 2.50 times as massive as sample 1, so it contains 2.50 × 1.20 g = 3.00 g of carbon.
questions.working: By the law of definite proportions, the mass of C is proportional to the mass of CO₂: 1.20 g × (11.0 g/4.40 g) = 1.20 g × 2.50 = 3.00 g. (Check: 12.01/44.01 = 27.3% C; 0.273 × 11.0 g = 3.00 g.)

options: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4

questions.q: A mixture of 1.00 g of NaCl and 4.00 g of sand, which contains no chlorine, is 12.1% chlorine by mass. Another 1.00 g of NaCl is added to the mixture and mixed in. What is the mass percent of chlorine in the new mixture?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a mixture has a fixed composition picks this. Adding NaCl changes the proportions: the mixture now contains 1.213 g of chlorine in 6.00 g, or 20.2%.
NaCl is 60.66% chlorine by mass, so 2.00 g of NaCl contains 1.213 g of Cl. The new mixture has a total mass of 6.00 g, so it is 1.213/6.00 = 20.2% chlorine by mass.

A student who thinks doubling the NaCl doubles the mass percent of chlorine picks this. The mass of chlorine doubles, but the total mass also increases, from 5.00 g to 6.00 g, so the percentage rises only to 20.2%.
A student who gives the mixture the composition of pure NaCl picks this. The sand adds 4.00 g of mass but no chlorine, so the mixture is only 20.2% chlorine.
questions.explain: NaCl is 60.66% chlorine by mass, so 2.00 g of NaCl contains 1.213 g of Cl. The new mixture has a total mass of 6.00 g, so it is 1.213/6.00 = 20.2% chlorine by mass.
questions.working: Mass fraction of Cl in NaCl = 35.45/58.44 = 0.6066. New mixture: 2.00 g NaCl contains 2.00 × 0.6066 = 1.213 g Cl; total mass = 2.00 + 4.00 = 6.00 g. Mass percent Cl = 1.213/6.00 × 100% = 20.2%.

questions.q: A 2.00 g sample of impure potassium chloride, KCl, is found by elemental analysis to contain 0.855 g of chlorine. The impurity contains no chlorine. In addition to these data, which information does a student need in order to calculate the percent purity of the KCl?
options: The mass percent of Cl in KCl, from molar masses
None; the percent purity is 0.855 g ÷ 2.00 g × 100%
The number of atoms in one formula unit of KCl
The identity and the molar mass of the impurity
optionWhy: The chlorine is part of the KCl, so its mass must be converted to the mass of KCl: mass of KCl = 0.855 g ÷ (35.45/74.55) = 1.80 g. The purity is then 1.80/2.00 = 89.9%.
A student who takes the mass of chlorine to be the mass of KCl picks this. 0.855 g ÷ 2.00 g gives the mass percent of chlorine in the sample (42.8%), not of KCl; the KCl also contains potassium.

A student who thinks the mass fraction of an element equals its fraction of the atoms picks this. Cl is half of the atoms in KCl but 47.55% of its mass; the molar masses, not the number of atoms, are needed.

A student who thinks the impurity must always be identified picks this. The impurity contains no chlorine, so all the chlorine is in KCl, and the mass of KCl can be found without knowing what the impurity is.
questions.explain: The chlorine is part of the KCl, so its mass must be converted to the mass of KCl: mass of KCl = 0.855 g ÷ (35.45/74.55) = 1.80 g. The purity is then 1.80/2.00 = 89.9%.
questions.working: Mass fraction of Cl in KCl = 35.45/74.55 = 0.4755. Mass of KCl = 0.855 g ÷ 0.4755 = 1.80 g. Purity = 1.80/2.00 × 100% = 89.9%. The quantity needed is the mass percent of Cl in pure KCl (from the molar masses).

questions.q: The diagram shows a shell model of a neutral atom in its ground state. How many core electrons and how many valence electrons does the atom have?
options: Core 10, valence 5
Core 2, valence 13
Core 12, valence 3
Core 10, valence 3
optionWhy: The valence electrons are the 5 electrons in the outermost occupied shell. The core electrons are the electrons in the shells inside it: 2 + 8 = 10.
A student who thinks core electrons are only those in the innermost shell picks this. The eight electrons in the second shell are also inner electrons, so there are 10 core electrons.

A student who thinks valence electrons are only those in the last-filled subshell (3p³) picks this. The two 3s electrons are also in the outermost shell, so there are 5 valence electrons and 10 core electrons.
A student who takes the number of valence electrons to be the number needed to fill the outer shell (8 − 5 = 3) picks this. Valence electrons are the outer electrons the atom has: 5.
questions.explain: The valence electrons are the 5 electrons in the outermost occupied shell. The core electrons are the electrons in the shells inside it: 2 + 8 = 10.
questions.working: The outermost occupied shell holds 5 electrons, so there are 5 valence electrons. The two inner shells hold 2 + 8 = 10 core electrons. Total 15, equal to the nuclear charge.

questions.q: A ground-state aluminum atom has the electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹. How does the energy required to remove a 2p electron from the atom compare with the energy required to remove the 3p electron?
options: It is the same for both, since one nucleus attracts each of its electrons with equal force.
It is greater for the 3p electron, as an electron in a higher energy level needs more energy to leave.
It is smaller for a 2p electron, since six 2p electrons share an attraction that 3p has alone.
It is greater for a 2p electron, which is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer electrons.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a nucleus attracts all of its electrons equally picks this. The attraction depends on each electron's distance from the nucleus and on the electrons that shield it, and both differ for 2p and 3p.
A student who confuses the energy of an electron with the energy needed to remove it picks this. An electron in a higher energy level is held less strongly, so less energy is required to remove it.

A student who thinks the attraction of the nucleus is shared out among the electrons of a subshell picks this. The force on each electron is given by Coulomb's law and is not divided; the 2p electrons are closer and less shielded, so each is held more strongly.

A 2p electron is in the second shell, closer to the nucleus than the 3p electron, and only the two 1s electrons lie inside it. By Coulomb's law it is attracted more strongly, so more energy is required to remove it.
questions.explain: A 2p electron is in the second shell, closer to the nucleus than the 3p electron, and only the two 1s electrons lie inside it. By Coulomb's law it is attracted more strongly, so more energy is required to remove it.

questions.q: An ion has a charge of 1−, contains 18 electrons and has a mass number of 37. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a nucleus has equal numbers of protons and neutrons picks this, after finding 17 protons. The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the number of protons: 37 − 17 = 20.
A student who reads the 1− charge as one electron lost picks this, giving the nucleus 19 protons and 37 − 19 = 18 neutrons. A negative ion has one more electron than protons, so there are 17 protons.
A student who takes the number of protons to equal the number of electrons picks this: 37 − 18 = 19. The ion has a 1− charge, so it has one fewer proton than electrons, 17.
The ion has one more electron than protons, so it has 18 − 1 = 17 protons. The mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons, so there are 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.
questions.explain: The ion has one more electron than protons, so it has 18 − 1 = 17 protons. The mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons, so there are 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.
questions.working: Charge = protons − electrons, so protons = 18 − 1 = 17. Neutrons = mass number − protons = 37 − 17 = 20.

questions.q: The complete photoelectron spectrum of an element is shown. According to the spectrum, how many electrons does an atom of the element have in the subshell from which an electron is most easily removed?
optionWhy: A student who thinks each electron gives its own peak picks this, taking the right-hand peak to be a single electron. The height of a peak shows how many electrons share that binding energy; the right-hand peak has height 3.

A student who reads the left-hand peak as the electrons easiest to remove picks this, reading the height of the peak at about 208 MJ/mol. That peak is at the highest binding energy, the 1s electrons, which are the hardest to remove.

The binding-energy axis increases to the left, so the least tightly held electrons give the right-hand peak, at about 1.01 MJ/mol. Its relative height is 3, so that subshell (3p in this element, phosphorus, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³) contains three electrons.

A student who thinks a p-subshell peak always stands for six electrons picks this. The right-hand peak belongs to the 3p subshell, but its height, 3, shows that the subshell contains only three electrons; six is its capacity.
questions.explain: The binding-energy axis increases to the left, so the least tightly held electrons give the right-hand peak, at about 1.01 MJ/mol. Its relative height is 3, so that subshell (3p in this element, phosphorus, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³) contains three electrons.
questions.working: Binding energy increases to the left, so the most easily removed electrons give the right-hand peak, at about 1.01 MJ/mol. Its relative height is 3, so that subshell contains 3 electrons. (Reading all five peaks, 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 3, gives 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, phosphorus; the 3p subshell holds the most easily removed electrons.)

questions.q: In the photoelectron spectrum of lithium, the 1s peak is at 6.26 MJ/mol and the 2s peak is at 0.52 MJ/mol. Which statement best supports the claim that a lithium atom holds its 1s electrons much more strongly than its 2s electron?
options: The 1s peak is twice as tall as the 2s peak, so it shows electrons that need more energy to remove.
The 1s subshell is filled, so its electrons are more stable than the single electron in the 2s subshell.
The 1s electrons are removed after the 2s electron, so each needs more energy than the electron before it.
The 1s electrons are much closer to the nucleus, so the nucleus attracts them much more strongly.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a taller peak shows electrons that need more energy picks this. The 1s peak is twice as tall because the 1s subshell holds two electrons and the 2s subshell one; the energy needed is shown by the position of the peak, 6.26 MJ/mol compared with 0.52 MJ/mol.

A student who thinks a filled subshell holds its electrons more tightly because it is filled picks this. How strongly an electron is held depends on its Coulombic attraction to the nucleus, which is far greater for the 1s electrons because they are much closer to it.

A student who thinks each electron needs more energy than the one removed before it picks this. In photoelectron spectroscopy each electron is ejected from a separate neutral atom, so the 1s peak shows the energy needed to remove a 1s electron from a lithium atom, not from an ion that has already lost its 2s electron.

By Coulomb's law the attraction between the nucleus and an electron increases as the distance between them decreases. The 1s electrons are, on average, much closer to the nucleus than the 2s electron, and no electrons lie between them and the nucleus, so they need far more energy to remove.
questions.explain: By Coulomb's law the attraction between the nucleus and an electron increases as the distance between them decreases. The 1s electrons are, on average, much closer to the nucleus than the 2s electron, and no electrons lie between them and the nucleus, so they need far more energy to remove.

questions.q: Which description of the complete photoelectron spectrum of a ground-state silicon atom is correct?
options: Three peaks, one for each of the occupied shells
Five peaks, with the 2p peak tallest of all
Fourteen peaks, each of the same height
Five peaks, with the 1s peak the tallest
optionWhy: A student who thinks all of the electrons in a shell have the same energy picks this, expecting one peak for each of the three occupied shells. Electrons in different subshells of the same shell need different energies to remove, so the 2s and 2p electrons, and the 3s and 3p electrons, give separate peaks.

Si is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p². Each of the five occupied subshells gives one peak, and the heights are proportional to the numbers of electrons, 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 2, so the 2p peak, for six electrons, is the tallest.

A student who thinks each electron gives its own peak picks this, expecting one peak for each of the 14 electrons. All of the electrons in one subshell share one binding energy and are counted in a single peak, so there are five peaks of different heights.

A student who thinks a taller peak shows electrons that need more energy to remove picks this, because the 1s electrons are the hardest to remove. The 1s peak is at the highest binding energy, but its height corresponds to two electrons; the 2p peak, for six electrons, is the tallest.
questions.explain: Si is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p². Each of the five occupied subshells gives one peak, and the heights are proportional to the numbers of electrons, 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 2, so the 2p peak, for six electrons, is the tallest.

questions.q: The table gives the ground-state electron configurations of atoms of five elements labeled Q, R, T, X and Z. Which two of the elements are in the same group of the periodic table?
options: Q and T
R and T
R and X
X and Z
optionWhy: A student who places every atom ending in two s electrons in group 2 picks this. Q (1s², helium) has a completely filled shell and is a noble gas; T (beryllium) has two valence electrons outside a filled 1s core.

A student who thinks elements with the same number of occupied shells are in the same group picks this. R and T both have two occupied shells, so they are in the same period, period 2, but they have one and two valence electrons respectively.
R (1s² 2s¹, lithium) and X (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹, sodium) each have one valence electron in an s subshell outside a filled-shell core, so both are in group 1.

A student who counts only the electrons in the last-filled subshell as valence electrons picks this, because X ends in 3s¹ and Z in 2p¹. Z (boron) has three valence electrons, 2s² 2p¹, so it is in group 13, while X is in group 1.
questions.explain: R (1s² 2s¹, lithium) and X (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹, sodium) each have one valence electron in an s subshell outside a filled-shell core, so both are in group 1.

questions.q: Which statement describes the process whose energy change is the first ionization energy of magnesium?
options: An atom in solid Mg loses two electrons, forming an aqueous Mg²⁺ ion
An atom in solid Mg loses one electron, forming a gaseous Mg⁺ ion
A gaseous Mg atom takes in one electron, forming a gaseous Mg⁻ ion
A gaseous Mg atom loses one electron, forming a gaseous Mg⁺ ion
optionWhy: A student who thinks ionization means forming the ion the element normally has picks this. The first ionization energy refers to removing one electron from a gaseous atom to form a gaseous 1+ ion.

A student who thinks ionization energy refers to the element in its usual state picks this. Starting from the solid would add the energy needed to separate a Mg atom from the metal; ionization energy is defined for gaseous atoms.
A student who treats ionization energy and electron affinity as the same process picks this. Adding an electron to a gaseous atom is the process of electron affinity; ionization removes an electron.
The first ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state, forming a gaseous 1+ ion.
questions.explain: The first ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state, forming a gaseous 1+ ion.
questions.working: First ionization: remove one electron from one gaseous atom in its ground state: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻. Charge balances (0 = +1 − 1) and the states are gaseous.
